questions.stem: As an engineer designing a simulation system, you frequently need to merge two large priority queues. If you use standard binary heaps, this UNION operation is a major bottleneck. According to the text, what is the worst-case running time of UNION for standard binary heaps, and how does a binomial heap improve it?
options: Binary heap: Θ(n), Binomial heap: O(lg n)
Binary heap: O(lg n), Binomial heap: O(1)
Binary heap: Θ(n), Binomial heap: O(1)
Binary heap: O(lg n), Binomial heap: O(lg n)
questions.explanation: The text states that by concatenating the arrays of two binary heaps and running MIN-HEAPIFY, UNION takes Θ(n) worst-case time, while binomial heaps perform UNION in O(lg n) time.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the distribution of nodes at depth i in a binomial tree Bk?
options: There are exactly (k choose i) nodes at depth i.
There are exactly 2^i nodes at depth i.
There are exactly k - i nodes at depth i.
There are exactly (k-1 choose i) nodes at depth i.
questions.explanation: Property 3 of Lemma 19.1 explicitly states that there are exactly (k choose i) nodes at depth i in binomial tree Bk, which also gives the 'binomial' tree its name.

questions.stem: It is a common misconception that because binomial trees grow exponentially in total size (2^k nodes), their maximum node degree must also grow very quickly as a function of n. Is it true that the maximum degree of any node in an n-node binomial tree is tightly bounded by lg n?
options: True
False
questions.explanation: According to Corollary 19.2, the maximum degree of any node in an n-node binomial tree is exactly lg n.

questions.stem: In a binomial heap H containing exactly 13 nodes, which specific binomial trees will be present in the heap?
options: B3, B2, and B0
B4 and B1
B3, B1, and B0
B2, B1, and B0
questions.explanation: The binary representation of 13 is 1101. As the text explains, binomial tree Bi appears in H if and only if bit i is 1. Thus, bit 3, bit 2, and bit 0 are 1, meaning B3, B2, and B0 are present.

questions.stem: How is each binomial tree within a binomial heap represented in memory to support efficient merge operations?
options: Using a left-child, right-sibling representation where each node points to its parent, leftmost child, and immediate right sibling.
Using an array-based representation identical to binary heaps, where a node at index i has children at 2i and 2i+1.
Using a doubly-linked list for all children of a node, with an explicit array of pointers to each child.
Using a binary search tree representation where the left child is smaller and the right child is larger than the parent.
questions.explanation: The text details that each binomial tree is stored in the left-child, right-sibling representation, where each node contains pointers p[x], child[x], and sibling[x].

questions.stem: During the BINOMIAL-LINK(y, z) procedure, how is a B_{k-1} tree rooted at y linked to a B_{k-1} tree rooted at z?
options: Node y becomes the new head of the linked list of node z's children, making z the root of a Bk tree.
Node z becomes the new head of the linked list of node y's children, making y the root of a Bk tree.
Node y is inserted as the rightmost sibling in node z's child list.
The roots y and z are both attached as children to a newly allocated dummy root node.
questions.explanation: BINOMIAL-LINK makes node z the parent of y, and y becomes the leftmost child of z (the new head of the linked list of z's children).

questions.stem: Imagine an 'Expanding Brain' meme comparing priority queue operations. Small brain: Rebuilding a binary heap from scratch in O(n) time. Galaxy brain: Uniting two binomial heaps in O(lg n) time. During this O(lg n) BINOMIAL-HEAP-UNION procedure, what dictates whether two roots are linked together?
options: They are linked if they have the same degree, using 4 distinct cases to maintain the property of having at most one root of each degree.
They are linked based solely on their key values, ensuring the smaller key is always placed to the left of the larger key.
They are linked only if they both belong to the same original input heap, maintaining strict separation until the final step.
They are linked randomly and then restructured later to satisfy the binomial heap properties.
questions.explanation: BINOMIAL-HEAP-UNION repeatedly links binomial trees whose roots have the same degree. The algorithm evaluates 4 specific cases based on the degrees of x, next-x, and sibling[next-x] to resolve duplicates.

questions.stem: Consider the analogy of opening a matryoshka (Russian nesting doll). When you remove the outer layer, you are left with a collection of perfectly intact smaller dolls. Similarly, in a binomial heap, when BINOMIAL-HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN removes the root of a Bk tree, what must be done to its children to prepare them for the UNION step?
options: The linked list of its children is reversed to form a new valid binomial heap, which is then united with the rest of the original heap.
The children are immediately re-inserted into the heap one by one using the standard INSERT procedure.
The children's degrees are all incremented by 1, and they are appended to the end of the root list.
The smallest child is promoted to become the new root of the entire Bk tree structure without altering the siblings.
questions.explanation: The children of a Bk root are roots of B_{k-1}, B_{k-2}, ..., B0 trees (in that order). To form a valid binomial heap, their linked list must be reversed so their degrees strictly increase, creating a new heap H' that can be passed to BINOMIAL-HEAP-UNION.

questions.stem: In the BINOMIAL-HEAP-DECREASE-KEY procedure, what happens if the decreased key of a node y becomes smaller than the key of its parent z?
options: The procedure exchanges the keys and satellite data of y and z, and continues 'bubbling up' the tree until the min-heap property is satisfied.
The procedure detaches node y and its subtree, moving it directly to the root list of the binomial heap.
The procedure recursively decreases the keys of all children of y to maintain the min-heap property.
The procedure performs a BINOMIAL-LINK on y and z to fuse them into a single node.
questions.explanation: Like a binary min-heap, BINOMIAL-HEAP-DECREASE-KEY 'bubbles up' the decreased key by repeatedly exchanging it with its parent's key until min-heap order is restored.

questions.stem: How does the BINOMIAL-HEAP-DELETE(H, x) procedure effectively remove a specific node x in O(lg n) time?
options: It decreases x's key to -∞ to bubble it to the root, and then extracts it using BINOMIAL-HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN.
It directly unlinks x from its parent and siblings, and then calls MIN-HEAPIFY on the affected trees.
It replaces x's key with the key of the last node in the heap, deletes the last node, and bubbles the new key down.
It splits the binomial tree containing x into two separate trees, discards x, and merges the remaining trees back into the heap.
questions.explanation: BINOMIAL-HEAP-DELETE first calls BINOMIAL-HEAP-DECREASE-KEY with a value of -∞ to bring node x to the root level, and then eliminates it entirely by calling BINOMIAL-HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN.
